answer: Main result: a single deterministic Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes multiplies two n-bit integers exactly in O(n(lg n)^{1-kappa}) worst-case time with kappa = 2^{-182}. Its time divided by n lg n tends to zero, so it refutes the conjecture of Schonhage and Strassen that n log n is the best possible order of growth in this model. Plan: the integer product is turned into a totipuv of short digit coefficients, and the tobifup turns a totipuv into pointwise multiplication. On a tape machine each transform level costs a full pass, so two primitives (chunk interchange and sifigeg) are made to cost volume times a power below one of their width: a call at parameter mf makes s < Wm smaller calls, using nested subspace labels on a fixed linear exchange network. These speed up the synthetic transforms and the ring convolution. Prime-length transforms are reduced to power-of-two ones by Sikusup and Bluestein chirps, with permutations kept inside the identities rather than executed. The exact 2n-bit product is then assembled by two forward transforms, a pointwise product, the opposite transform, rescaling, rounding and carry propagation, with total error below 1/2. Cost accounting divides every cost by the volume and shows that a power of lg n is saved.

A machine has a single finite alphabet and a finite number of one-dimensional tapes, both fixed independently of the input.
In 1971 Schönhage and Strassen gave a multiplication algorithm running in $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time, and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth.
The machine is deterministic, with a fixed finite alphabet and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes, and is correct for every $n\ge1$.
The multiplication reduces to transforms on arrays of polynomials over $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$, whose calculation consists of address rearrangements, signed shifts and two-point butterflies.
On a tape machine that is one pass over the whole stored volume of $\Theta(n)$ bits per level, so the levels cost $\Theta(n\log n)$.
